explanations: luna: The section's source dictionary joins the image (مِثال) with seeing and the lesson (مَثَل); this ayah's parable of a person lighting a fire ends with his light taken away and his inability to see, combining the image's two senses.

terra: The punished Sabbath-breakers are made a warning example for contemporaries and later people; this plausibly supports the source's م ث ل-as-lesson strand, though the ayah uses نَكَٰلًا rather than the named root.

luna: The section's human reads ample provision as honor; God's answer to Abraham grants even the disbeliever brief enjoyment before driving him to the punishment of the Fire, separating provision from approval.

luna: The section says provision and restriction are a test; this ayah explicitly names fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives, and fruits as tests, including the scarcity that the human misreads as humiliation. | terra: Fear, hunger, and loss are announced as forms of testing, giving deprivation an explicit purpose other than humiliation.
luna: After 2:155 names losses as a test, this ayah gives the response of those who say they belong to God and return to Him, rather than calling the test humiliation.
terra: The believers ask God to pour patience upon them, using ص ب ب for sustaining firmness before battle rather than for a scourge poured upon transgressors.
terra: The encounter of two armies is an عِبْرَةً for people of sight, showing a witnessed historical scene becoming inward lesson rather than visual report alone.

luna: The section makes ruined peoples an object for the reader's sight; this ayah tells people to travel the earth and look at how the deniers ended, turning movement through lands into witnessing their fate. | terra: The hearer is ordered to travel through the land and look at the deniers' end, making travelers deliberate observers of earlier judgments.

luna: The section's human reads ease as honor; this ayah warns disbelievers not to think that respite is good for them, since it only increases their sin, reversing the apparent meaning of worldly ease. | terra: Disbelievers must not read divine respite as good for themselves; the delay only lets sin increase before humiliating punishment, matching the watcher who waits rather than chases.
luna: The section makes human provision an ordeal misread as a verdict; this ayah says people will be tested in their wealth and lives, making the trial explicit.

luna: The section joins crossing the lands with people who mistake status for security; this ayah tells believers not to be deceived by the disbelievers' movement through the land, making their apparent power a false sign. | terra: The disbelievers' free movement through the lands must not deceive the observer, warning against reading unhindered travel as escape from the watcher.

luna: After 3:196 warns against being impressed by the disbelievers' movement, this ayah calls their enjoyment brief and their destination Hell, separating worldly ease from final honor. | terra: That movement is only brief enjoyment before Hell becomes their resting-place, completing 3:196's correction.
terra: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيْكُمْ رَقِيبًا states God's enduring watch over human relations, sharing the section's observer stance without the road setting.
terra: Jesus says that after God took him, God alone was the watcher over his people, locating complete observation with the divine speaker.

luna: The section joins country-crossing with observing what befell earlier peoples; this ayah directly commands travel through the earth and look at the end of the deniers. | terra: “Travel through the land, then look” at the deniers' end repeats the section's movement from route to perceptive seeing.

luna: The section says the traveler learns of the watcher when the blow falls; this ayah says people were given everything and rejoiced, then were seized suddenly after forgetting the warning, a direct account of false security under abundance. | terra: After people forget the warning, every gate of prosperity is opened; while they exult, they are seized suddenly, showing bounty immediately before the waiting blow.
terra: The keys of the unseen belong to God, who knows every falling leaf and hidden grain, expressing a watch from which neither movement nor concealed place escapes.
terra: God takes people by night, knows what they earn by day, and raises them until an appointed term before their return and accounting; night, observation, delay, and destination meet.
terra: God sends guardians over people until death and His messengers take the soul without neglect, a temporal watch that ends in the unavoidable encounter.

luna: The section's source dictionary connects the blow to a serpent dropping on its target from above; this ayah names punishment from above or beneath the feet, making the vertical attack an explicit divine threat. | terra: God can send punishment from above or beneath the feet, giving the section's overhead pounce a wider statement of inescapable directions.

luna: The section's human eye looks outward while the Lord watches the traveler; this ayah says eyes cannot encompass Him but He encompasses all eyes, setting the watcher beyond human sight. | terra: Human sights do not encompass God while He encompasses every sight, setting a precise boundary between the watched eye and the watcher it cannot see.
terra: Insights have come from the Lord; whoever sees does so for himself and whoever remains blind bears that loss, articulating the inward meaning of the observer command.

luna: The section says travelers learn of the watcher when the blow falls; this ayah recalls towns destroyed when punishment came at night or while their people slept, a direct scene of an unseen strike.

luna: The section's source dictionary form المِرْصاد is a road-side watchpoint; Iblis says he will sit on God's straight صِرَاط to obstruct its travelers, reversing the Lord's unseen watch into a declared hostile one. | terra: Iblis vows to sit for human beings on God's straight path; this is the section's stationary watcher waiting where every traveler must go.

luna: The section recalls peoples who crossed lands and exceeded their limits; this ayah says Thamud settled the plains and carved homes from mountains, then warns them not to spread corruption there.
luna: The section recalls what happened to Thamud after their boundary-breaking; this ayah says an earthquake seized them and they lay dead in their homes, another account of the sudden end.
terra: After the destructive rain, the hearer is told to look at the criminals' outcome, joining the descending blow to instructed observation.

luna: The section's source dictionary form المِرْصاد is where a watcher waits along a road; Shuʿayb forbids sitting at every صِرَاط to threaten passers and turn them aside, exposing the human version of the ambush. | terra: Shuʿayb forbids his people to sit threatening on every path and bar believers, a human enactment of the road turned into an ambush point.
terra: God first touches the people of towns with hardship and adversity so that they may humble themselves, establishing deprivation as purposeful testing rather than humiliation.
terra: Adversity is exchanged for prosperity, but their misreading is followed by a sudden seizure; the same two conditions culminate at the unseen watchpoint.

luna: The section says travelers learn of the watcher only when the blow falls; this ayah asks whether a town can feel secure from punishment arriving at night while its people sleep, matching the unseen night strike.

luna: The section's night traveler cannot see the waiting watcher; this neighboring warning asks whether people feel secure from punishment in daylight while they play, showing that no hour makes the passage safe.

luna: The section's Lord waits at the point people must pass; this ayah asks whether people feel secure from God's plan and denies that security, stating the inward mistake behind missing the watcher.
terra: Pharaoh's threatened believers ask their Lord to pour patience upon them, reversing the source's punitive pour while retaining descent from the true sovereign above Pharaoh.

luna: The section joins human communities spread through the lands with provision as a test; this ayah says people were divided into nations across the earth and tested with good and bad things. | terra: The scattered people are tested with good things and bad things so that they may return, another explicit single testing purpose behind opposite conditions.

luna: The section defines seeing as eye or insight; this ayah says some have eyes but do not see, alongside hearts that do not understand, naming the failure of perception behind the ruined peoples. | terra: People have hearts with which they do not understand and eyes with which they do not see, directly distinguishing possession of the eye from the insight demanded by the section.

luna: The section's watcher waits where people do not perceive him; this ayah says those who deny the signs will be drawn on gradually from where they do not know. | terra: Those denying the signs are led gradually toward destruction from where they do not know, a direct statement of the hidden watch disclosed only at the blow.

luna: After 7:182 describes the gradual approach unseen, this ayah says respite is given while God's plan is firm, explaining how security can conceal the approaching judgment. | terra: God grants the deniers respite because His plan is firm, completing 7:182's unnoticed approach to capture.

luna: The section's human reads material ease as honor; this ayah calls wealth and children a trial (فِتْنَة) and says the great reward is with God. | terra: Wealth and children are explicitly a trial, directly denying their use as a simple measure of honor.

luna: The section presents 9:5's ambush command against treaty-breakers; this preceding ayah exempts those who honored their treaties and orders the pact to be fulfilled, defining the boundary of the waiting punishment.

luna: The section's source root ر ص د gives المِرْصاد as a place where a watcher waits; the command to sit for the treaty-breakers at every مَرْصَد stages a human ambush on a route. | terra: The order to sit for treaty-breakers at كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍ uses the ر ص د place-word for an actual set of waiting positions on their routes.

luna: The section's human counts wealth as honor; this ayah tells the Prophet not to be impressed by disbelievers' wealth and children, which become a means of punishment for them. | terra: Wealth and children must not inspire admiration, because they can themselves belong to worldly punishment rather than signal divine favor.
terra: إِرْصَادًا describes a mosque established as an outpost for an enemy of God and His messenger, a different ر ص د use that still turns a fixed place into hostile waiting.
terra: Affliction makes a person call on God in every posture, but relief makes him pass on as though he never called, showing self-perception changing with circumstance.
terra: When people taste mercy after adversity they plot against the signs, while God's messengers record their plotting; changed provision, bad inward reading, and unseen observers coincide.
terra: No recitation or deed is entered without God being witness as people engage in it, and no smallest thing escapes Him; the watcher is present before actors notice an outcome.

luna: The section's night travelers pass along a route while the watcher waits; this ayah says Pharaoh pursued the Israelites across the sea until drowning caught him, reversing the roles of pursued and pursuer.
terra: When mercy is removed after being tasted, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful, explicitly treating deprivation as a final verdict.
terra: When blessing follows hardship, the human boasts that his troubles are gone, mirroring the opposite error about renewed abundance.
terra: Those who remain patient and do good are excepted from the despair and boasting in 11:9-10, marking the right response across both conditions.

luna: The section asks the reader to see what God did to a people; this ayah says the cry seized the wrongdoers of Thamud and left them fallen in their homes, a sudden end in the very land they inhabited.

luna: The section's source root س ر ي names a company moving by night; Lot is told to take his family out in part of the night, with his wife excepted from the escape. | terra: Lot is told to travel with his household during part of the night, not turn back, and trust a morning appointment; gaze, night route, and an inescapable descending judgment meet.
terra: The overturned town receives layered stones rained down from above, a close nonlexical parallel to the scourge poured onto transgressors.
terra: The seizure of unjust towns is a sign for one who fears the Hereafter, whose day is gathered and witnessed; observed past judgment points toward the universal watchpoint.
terra: People are asked whether they feel secure from an encompassing punishment or the Hour arriving suddenly while unaware, directly naming the unperceived encounter.

luna: The section shows the listener the fate of earlier peoples; this ayah asks whether people traveled through the land to see how those before ended, then contrasts the lasting home of the Hereafter. | terra: The question asks whether people have traveled in the land and seen the outcome of those before them, joining history's visible traces to judgment.
terra: The stories of the former peoples contain an عِبْرَةً for those with understanding, supporting the source's dictionary sense of مَثَل as a lesson drawn from what is narrated.
terra: Successive angels before and behind a person guard him by God's command; their stationed placement resembles 72:27 but functions as protection until a people change themselves.

luna: The section's human equates plenty with honor; this ayah says God extends and measures provision, then adds that people rejoice in worldly life although its enjoyment is small beside the Hereafter. | terra: God expands and restricts provision, while people rejoice in the nearer life although it is slight beside the Hereafter; this identifies the valuation behind the false honor reading.
luna: The section pictures the Lord waiting at the point every traveler must cross; this ayah describes Him as قائم over every soul for what it earns, making the watch continual and personal.
terra: God is not unaware of what wrongdoers do; He only delays them to a day when eyes stare, expressing the watcher who waits rather than immediately chasing.
terra: On that delayed day they rush forward with heads raised and gaze unable to return, making the watched travelers' own eyes part of the judgment announced in 14:42.
terra: The audience dwells in the homes of wrongdoers, has been shown how God dealt with them, and has received examples; route, sight, divine action, and م ث ل-as-lesson converge.
luna: The section links the watcher root ر ص د to a flame lying in wait in the sky; this ayah says the sky is guarded from every accursed devil, setting up the same celestial watch.
luna: The section says a jinn who listens finds a flame lying in wait; this ayah says a devil who snatches a hearing is pursued by a clear flame, specifying the same interception.

luna: The section's source root س ر ي describes night travel; Lot is commanded to travel with his family during part of the night and keep moving as instructed. | terra: Lot is commanded to set out in a portion of the night, follow behind his people, forbid backward looks, and proceed where ordered, an exact night-traveler scene disciplined by sight.
luna: Following Lot's night-escape command in 15:65, this ayah tells him the people will be cut off in the morning, setting the dangerous passage against the fate awaiting those left behind.
terra: The destroyed towns contain signs for careful observers, ٱلْمُتَوَسِّمِينَ, naming the discriminating gaze the section asks of its listener.
terra: The ruins lie on an enduring, established road, so the lesson in 15:75 is literally waiting where travelers pass.
terra: The road-side ruins in 15:76 are declared a sign for believers, stating what the observer is meant to gain from the scene.

luna: The section invites the reader to see what happened to earlier peoples; this passage names the people of al-Ḥijr, who denied the messengers, locating another ruined community on the route through the land. | terra: The People of al-Ḥijr deny the messengers, naming the historical community behind the rock-cutting Thamūd scene while also sounding the source's h-j-r word.

luna: The section makes the reader an observer of a people's fate; this ayah says the people of al-Ḥijr were given signs yet turned away, connecting sight to failure to take warning. | terra: God gives the People of al-Ḥijr signs but they turn away, clarifying the failure of perception before their secure dwellings and seizure in 15:82-83.

luna: The section's Thamud cut through rock in the valley; this ayah says the people of al-Ḥijr carved secure homes into the mountains, developing the same rock-cut habitation. | terra: Thamūd carve secure houses from mountains, a close counterpart to their cutting rock in the valley and confidence in works along the land.

luna: The section places the blow before it names the watchpoint; this ayah says a cry seized the people of al-Ḥijr in the morning, making the sudden punishment visible. | terra: The blast takes those supposedly secure rock-carvers at morning, turning their built route and refuge into the point of capture.

luna: The section recalls the works of the people who crossed the land; this ayah says what they had earned did not avail them when the punishment came, reversing confidence in their built homes. | terra: What Thamūd earned avails them nothing, completing the observed reversal of apparent security in 15:82-83.

terra: God attacks plotters' building from its foundations so the roof falls on them from above and punishment comes from where they do not perceive, closely reproducing the hidden watcher and overhead pounce.

luna: The section recalls the outcome of transgressors; this ayah sends people to travel the land and see the end of those who denied the messengers. | terra: After messengers confront every nation, people are told to travel and see the deniers' end, a direct route from transgression to observed consequence.

luna: The section's watcher waits where the traveler cannot avoid passing; this ayah asks whether plotters feel safe from being swallowed by the earth or struck from where they do not perceive. | terra: Those plotting evil are asked whether they feel secure from being swallowed by earth or seized from where they do not perceive.

luna: The section's watcher does not need to pursue a traveler; this ayah says God may seize plotters while they go about and they cannot escape, making ordinary movement no protection. | terra: God may seize them during their movement about, and they cannot frustrate Him; the travelers' motion does not evade the waiting judgment of 16:45.
terra: God may take wrongdoers gradually amid fear, extending 16:45-46's sudden and movement-time seizures with a slower form of the same inescapable watch.
terra: God delays people to an appointed term rather than seizing them immediately for wrongdoing, another explicit account of the watcher waiting until the fixed point.
terra: People emerge from the womb knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts so they may give thanks, stating the intended use of the eye's gift.

luna: The section's human reads plenty as honor and scarcity as humiliation; this ayah offers the example of a secure town given abundant provision, then made to taste hunger and fear after ingratitude. | terra: A secure town with abundant provision becomes ungrateful and is made to taste encompassing hunger and fear, directly overturning abundance as proof of lasting honor.

luna: Following the secure, well-provided town's punishment in 16:112, this ayah says a messenger came from among them but they denied him, identifying the refusal behind the change from provision to fear.

luna: The section's source root س ر ي concerns night travel; this ayah says God carried His servant by night, a guided journey rather than the threatened escape of Lot and Moses. | terra: The night journey of God's servant from the Sacred Mosque to the farthest mosque is the Quran's signal occurrence of the source's س ر ي night-travel sense.

luna: The section turns the gaze inward after showing a people's fate; this ayah says each person's record is fixed to him and will be brought forth on Judgment Day, preparing the self-reading of 17:14.

luna: The section shifts from looking at earlier peoples to looking at oneself; this ayah tells each person to read his own record, making the observed person his own reckoner. | terra: The person is told to read his own record and is sufficient as a reckoner against himself, a judgment-day form of inward self-observation.

luna: The section shows a person mistaking worldly provision for honor; this ayah says one who desires the immediate life may receive it, but ends by warning of Hell, so immediate abundance does not certify divine approval.

luna: The section contrasts a human's reading of present provision with his final state; this ayah describes the believer who seeks the Hereafter and strives for it, giving the other orientation to life.
luna: After distinguishing those who seek the Hereafter in 17:19, this ayah says God provides to both groups from His gift, showing that worldly provision alone does not mark approval.

luna: This ayah asks the reader to look at how some are favored over others in worldly life, then says the Hereafter has greater degrees and preference, directly correcting the section's status judgment.

luna: The section contrasts the human's claim of honor with restricted provision; this ayah says the Lord extends or measures provision for whom He wills and is seeing of His servants, placing both conditions under a watchful giver. | terra: God expands and restricts provision while being fully aware and seeing of His servants, correcting the human who treats those two measures as honor and humiliation.
terra: Hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned, turning the faculties that failed ʿĀd into accountable witnesses.
terra: Favor makes the human turn away in self-importance, while evil makes him despair, a concise statement of the same two mistaken reactions to one Lord's testing.
luna: The section gives مَثَل the secondary sense of an instructive lesson; this ayah says every kind of example has been presented in the Qur'an, yet most people persist in disbelief.
luna: The section's human reads a favorable worldly condition as honor; this ayah says earthly adornment is a test of who acts best, directly naming the purpose of visible plenty.
luna: After 18:7 calls earthly adornment a test, this ayah says the earth will be made barren ground, showing what remains when the visible provision passes.

luna: The section's human calls himself honored when provision is ample; the owner of the two gardens says he has more wealth and followers than his companion, voicing the same verdict from possessions. | terra: The garden-owner measures himself as greater in wealth and followers, beginning a self-image constructed from visible abundance.

luna: The section's human reads wealth as lasting honor; the garden owner enters his garden while wronging himself and says he does not think it will ever perish, showing how abundance conceals its limit. | terra: He enters his garden while wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, turning prosperity into imagined permanent security.

luna: The section's wealthy person mistakes present ease for honor; the garden owner assumes that if returned to his Lord he will receive something better, carrying the same worldly measure into the Hereafter. | terra: He doubts the Hour and expects an even better return if brought to his Lord, extending the false wealth-to-honor inference into the Hereafter.

luna: The section's man judges himself by wealth; his companion asks why he did not acknowledge God upon entering the garden, then notes his own lesser wealth and children, exposing the comparison by possessions.

luna: The section's abundant person takes his condition as honor; the companion says God may give him something better than the garden, then turn the garden into barren ground, exposing provision's impermanence.

luna: The section's human reads a prosperous condition as honor; after his garden is ruined, its owner turns his hands over what he spent and recognizes the loss, a reversal of confidence in lasting provision. | terra: His produce is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, the visible collapse that corrects his judgments in 18:34-36.
luna: The section's powerful people cannot outrun the watchpoint; after the garden is ruined, its owner has no group to help him against God.
luna: The section's human attributes honor to his own abundance; this ayah says true protection and authority belong to God, the right in whom to hope.
luna: The section's source dictionary gives مَثَل the sense of lesson; this ayah compares worldly life to rain-fed growth that becomes dry debris, a concrete image of provision that passes.
luna: The section's human judges honor by ample provision; this ayah calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life but says enduring good deeds are better with the Lord, replacing that measure.

luna: The section's watcher attends to what every person does; this ayah says the record is set out and leaves nothing small or great uncounted, making the hidden record visible at judgment. | terra: The placed record omits neither small nor great deed, and wrongdoers find what they did present before them, the exhaustive evidence gathered by the watchers.
terra: Every one of the addressed people will come to Hell by an irrevocable decree, closely matching the watchpoint placed on a route every traveler must meet.
terra: After everyone comes to the appointed place in 19:71, God saves the mindful and leaves wrongdoers kneeling, marking the moral boundary within the common route.
terra: The singular command to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed,” frames the same transgressor as the object of a divine mission before his capture.

luna: The section's source root ط غ ي names crossing a limit; Moses and Aaron are told to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, repeating the section's diagnosis of the ruler. | terra: Moses and Aaron together receive the command to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, repeating the stance with two witnesses sent to the limit-crosser.

luna: The section's source root س ر ي describes people traveling at night; Moses is commanded to take the Children of Israel by night (فَأَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي), and God opens a dry path through the sea for them. | terra: Moses is commanded to take the servants by night and strike a dry path through the sea without fear of being overtaken, combining night travel, a necessary route, and a waiting pursuer.

luna: The section's night travelers must pass through a route they do not control; as the continuation of 20:77, Pharaoh follows them into the sea and is overwhelmed, reversing who survives the crossing. | terra: Pharaoh follows them onto that path and the sea overwhelms him, revealing the route itself as the place where the transgressor is caught.
terra: Israel is warned not to transgress in good provision lest divine anger descend; abundance can be received within bounds or turn into the blow by crossing them.
terra: The Prophet is told not to stretch his eyes toward worldly splendor given to groups as a test, and that his Lord's provision is better and more lasting.

luna: The section describes plenty and scarcity as tests (ابتلاه); this ayah states directly that God tests people with evil and good (نَبْلُوكُم بِالشَّرِّ وَالْخَيْرِ فِتْنَةً), so neither condition by itself means honor or humiliation. | terra: Good and evil alike are tests before return to God, directly correcting the division of one trial into “honor” and “humiliation.”

luna: The section's human misjudges provision as honor or humiliation; this ayah says just scales will be set on the Day of Resurrection and no soul will be wronged, giving a measured judgment that does not follow worldly appearance.
terra: Abraham asks his people about هَٰذِهِ ٱلتَّمَاثِيلُ; these literal statues instantiate the source dictionary's م ث ل form-word, distinct from its lesson sense.
terra: The one who worships on an edge is content when good comes but turns away under a trial, enacting the section's division of one divine testing into two opposite verdicts.
terra: Boiling water is poured مِن فَوْقِ رُءُوسِهِمْ, making the section's ص ب ب movement an explicit punishment descending from above.

luna: The section's travelers cross lands marked by the ruins of former peoples; this ayah depicts destroyed townships with collapsed roofs, abandoned wells, and tall palaces left empty. | terra: Ruined towns, fallen roofs, abandoned wells, and lofty palaces supply the visible objects travelers should read with their hearts in 22:46.

luna: The section's source root رءي means seeing with eye or insight; this ayah asks people to travel and reason, then says blindness is in hearts rather than eyes, making observation a test of perception. | terra: Travel through the land should produce hearts that reason and ears that hear, for it is hearts rather than eyes that go blind; this unites the section's travelers, ruins, and inward sight.

luna: The section's human reads wealth as proof of being honored; this ayah asks whether provision of wealth and children is what the people think it is, opening a direct challenge to that reading. | terra: The question asks whether wealth and sons are being read as God hastening good to their owners, exactly exposing the section's prosperity-equals-honor inference.

luna: The section presents wealth as a test misread as honor; this ayah rejects the assumption that God is hastening good to people by giving them wealth and children, marking provision as no guarantee of favor. | terra: بَل لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ denies that inference as a failure of perception, completing the question in 23:55.
terra: God originates hearing, sights, and hearts, yet little thanks is given, another boundary between being equipped to see and actually responding.
terra: Tongues, hands, and feet testify to what their owners did, turning familiar bodily instruments into ready witnesses.

luna: The section's source dictionary links مِثَال (image) with seeing; this ayah develops a visible parable of light, a niche, glass, and a brilliant star, showing the Qur'an's image-language as a means of perception.
terra: One driven cloud yields rain and hail that God strikes or averts, while its lightning nearly takes sight; provision, selective overhead blow, and the vulnerable eye occupy one scene.
terra: God's alternation of night and day contains an عِبْرَةً for people of sight, joining the passing night to perceptive seeing rather than mere eyesight.
terra: When criminals see the angels they receive no good news and cry حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا; seeing and the source's h-j-r boundary-word coincide at judgment.
terra: Examples are set forth for each rejecting people before each is destroyed utterly, binding م ث ل to the observed consequences of collective transgression.
terra: The addressees have passed repeatedly by the town rained upon with evil rain, yet failed to see it; travelers literally cross a punishment-site without gaining the inward lesson.
terra: A barrier and حِجْرًا مَّحْجُورًا keep two bodies of water apart, giving the source's h-j-r eye-enclosure a Quranic boundary scene on a larger scale.

luna: The section's source root س ر ي names those who travel at night; Moses receives the same command to take God's servants by night before Pharaoh pursues them. | terra: God tells Moses to take His servants by night because they will be pursued, placing the traveling group and its would-be catcher on the same route.
luna: The section says Thamud cut through rock in a valley; this ayah describes them carving homes from mountains with skill, an explicit parallel to the rock-cut scene.
luna: The section names the people who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says the extravagant corrupters do not reform the earth, giving the root's overstepping a social consequence.
terra: An evil rain falls upon Lot's people, another punishment descending on those who had crossed their moral limit.
terra: Solomon sees the throne settled before him and names the favor a test of gratitude rather than proof of personal honor.
terra: Thamūd's conspirators swear to make a night attack on Ṣāliḥ and his family, setting up human watchers who believe they control the unseen strike.
terra: They plot while God counters their plot without their perceiving it, reversing the apparent watcher and the true watcher before the blow in 27:51.
terra: The hearer is told to look at the plotters' outcome: they and their people are destroyed, making the hidden counter-watch visible only in its result.
terra: The rain upon Lot's people is called evil for those already warned, emphasizing that the blow arrives after notice yet still overtakes them.

luna: The section makes the reader witness the end of overreaching peoples; this ayah tells people to travel the land and see the end of the guilty. | terra: The command to travel through the land and observe the criminals' outcome makes the listener a mobile witness of divine action.

luna: The section names Pharaoh among rulers who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says he exalted himself in the land, divided its people, and was among the corrupters, making the transgression concrete.
terra: Many towns exulting in their livelihood are destroyed and left as scarcely inhabited dwellings, making prosperity's false reading visible in ruins to later observers.
luna: The section's person reads what he has been given as honor; this ayah says worldly provision and adornment are temporary and what is with God is better and more lasting.
luna: After 28:60 contrasts worldly provision with what lasts, this ayah asks whether the one promised a good outcome is like the one merely enjoying worldly life before being brought to judgment.
luna: The section shows the human assessing himself through wealth; Qarun is given treasures so heavy that their keys burden a group of strong men, making his material standing visible.

luna: The section shows provision being misread as personal rank; this ayah tells Qarun to use what God gave him for the Hereafter and not to seek corruption in the land, giving the right response to abundance.
luna: The section's human claims that abundance means honor; Qarun says he received his wealth because of knowledge, repeating the self-crediting claim that 39:49 also exposes.

luna: The section makes the human's gaze on abundance the subject; Qarun goes out in adornment, and those who desire worldly life wish for what he was given, showing how visible wealth teaches the wrong lesson. | terra: Qārūn emerges in adornment and observers longing for worldly life call his share mighty fortune, staging the first, wealth-centered look later corrected in 28:82.

luna: The section describes abundance mistaken for honor; the people of knowledge answer Qarun's admirers that God's reward is better for those who believe and do right, setting a different measure. | terra: Those given knowledge answer the dazzled observers that God's reward is better, supplying insight before Qārūn's visible collapse.

luna: The section's watcher and punishment make the apparent security of the powerful unstable; the earth swallows Qarun and his house, ending the display of wealth without a rescuer. | terra: Qārūn and his house are swallowed by the earth with no rescuing faction; the sudden blow produces the changed sight confessed in 28:82.

luna: The section's human sees abundance as honor; after Qarun's wealth ends in ruin, the onlookers recognize that God extends and measures provision for whom He wills, overturning their earlier envy. | terra: Those who had wished for Qārūn's place now recognize that God expands and restricts provision; the sight of his collapse in 28:81 corrects their former reading of wealth.

luna: The section names those who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says the Hereafter's home is for those who do not seek exaltation or corruption on earth, marking the boundary opposite their overreach.

luna: The section shows the Lord's act on ʿĀd and Thamud and develops the path as a site of obstruction; this ayah says their dwellings remain visible, while Satan made their deeds pleasing and turned them from the path despite their perception. | terra: The dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamūd remain apparent, yet Satan barred them from the path although they were مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ; visible ruins, blocked road, and failed insight meet in one ayah.
terra: Qārūn, Pharaoh, and Hāmān act arrogantly in the land but cannot outrun God, answering the section's country-crossers with a limit no traveler can pass.
terra: Each people is seized for its sin by a distinct calamity, including a stone-storm and earth swallowing, making the unseen watch visible as precisely fitted blows.

luna: The section's source dictionary links مَثَل with an instructive example; this ayah says such parables are set forth for people, though only those who know understand them. | terra: God sets forth examples for humankind, but only those with knowledge understand them; the source's “parable as lesson” depends on inward perception.

luna: The section says people discover the watcher at the blow; this ayah says punishment will come suddenly while they are unaware, despite their demand that it be hastened. | terra: Punishment has an appointed time and will come suddenly while its subjects do not perceive, closely matching travelers learning of the watcher only when struck.

luna: The section's fixed watchpoint makes the travelers' route lead into judgment; this ayah says Hell will encompass the disbelievers, completing the warning of sudden punishment in 29:53. | terra: While they demand punishment be hastened, Hell already encompasses the disbelievers; this supplies the unseen surrounding reality behind 29:53's sudden arrival.

luna: The section's dictionary note describes a serpent striking from above; this ayah depicts punishment covering people from above and from beneath their feet, turning the hidden strike into an inescapable enclosure.
terra: God expands and restricts provision and knows all things, separating measured livelihood from the person's estimate of his own standing.
terra: People are asked whether they reflect within themselves before 30:9 asks them to travel and see former peoples' end, explicitly pairing inward and outward observation.

luna: The section recalls peoples who crossed lands and exceeded limits; this ayah asks people to travel and see the end of predecessors, noting their greater strength and the messengers' clear signs. | terra: Those who fail to travel and see the stronger former peoples' end repeat the blindness of ʿĀd despite visible cultivation and ruins.
terra: People rejoice when made to taste mercy and immediately despair when harm from their own deeds reaches them, repeating the divided reading of opposed conditions.

luna: The section's person looks at his provision and draws a verdict about himself; this ayah asks whether people see that God extends and measures provision, naming the allocation itself as a sign. | terra: أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا۟ introduces the same fact that God expands and restricts provision, making right seeing the cure for the section's mistaken twofold judgment.

luna: The section makes past peoples' fate visible; this ayah commands travel through the earth and observe the end of those before, most of whom associated partners with God. | terra: Travel and look at the earlier people's end is again commanded, with their associationism naming the moral reading of the remains.

luna: The section's source dictionary connects مَثَل with a lesson; this ayah says examples are set out for people, but disbelievers reject the sign, matching the failure to see a lesson in the section's history.
terra: God gives the fashioned human hearing, sight, and hearts, yet people give little thanks; the faculties exist before their inward use succeeds.
terra: God is watcher over every thing, extending the road-side image into universal surveillance.
terra: Not even an atom in heaven or earth escapes the Lord, and all is in a clear record; hidden movement and recorded observation are joined.
terra: The question asks whether people see what surrounds them of sky and earth before warning of earth swallowing or fragments falling from above; sight, enclosure, and the blow meet directly.
terra: The jinn make تَمَٰثِيلَ for Solomon, another concrete Quranic use of the source dictionary's “timsāl, an image,” without the idolatrous stance of 21:52.
terra: Travelers are told to journey through closely spaced settlements by night or day in safety, the positive opposite of a road occupied by an ambusher.
luna: The section's person judges himself honored by abundance; these leaders say they have more wealth and children and therefore will not be punished, making that same inference explicit.

luna: The section's human reads provision as rank; this ayah says God extends and measures provision as He wills, while most people do not know, correcting the inference. | terra: God expands and restricts provision, though most people do not know; the two economic states therefore cannot bear the two judgments the human assigns them.

luna: The section shows wealth being mistaken for honor; this ayah says neither wealth nor children bring people nearer to God, except faith and right action, reversing the measure of status. | terra: Wealth and children do not bring anyone nearer to God, explicitly severing abundance from the honor presumed in 34:35-36.
terra: The repeated expansion and restriction of provision belongs to the Lord, while spending is replaced by Him; both states remain acts of provision rather than verdicts on worth.
terra: A person whose evil deed is beautified so that he sees it as good gives a direct Quranic case of the inward eye manufacturing a false judgment.

luna: The section's observer is asked to see what happened to old peoples; this ayah asks whether people traveled and saw the end of those before them, who were stronger yet could not escape God. | terra: Travel should reveal the end of peoples stronger than the audience, showing that power cannot carry a traveler past God's grasp.
terra: God delays creatures to an appointed term instead of taking them at once for what they earn; when the term comes, He has always been seeing His servants.
terra: A barrier before and behind encloses people and covers them so they cannot see; the source's eye-enclosure becomes here an external enclosure that defeats eyesight.

luna: The section moves from observing others to one's own state; this ayah says mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what people did. | terra: Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what was earned, revealing that the traveler's own body has preserved the watch.
luna: The section's sky contains a watcher flame for a listener; this ayah says devils cannot listen to the highest assembly and are pelted from every side, giving the watch its purpose.
luna: The section describes a flame waiting for the one who tries to listen; this ayah says the devils are driven away and face lasting punishment, continuing that intercepted passage.
luna: The section's jinn meets a waiting flame while listening; this ayah allows only a thief who snatches a fragment of hearing, then says a piercing flame pursues him.
terra: The wrongdoers are directed to صِرَٰطِ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, turning the road itself toward Hell; 37:24 supplies the halt on that road.
terra: “Stop them; they are to be questioned” stages the unavoidable checkpoint at the end of the path named in 37:23.
terra: The Meccans pass the destroyed people of Lot in the morning, making the old judgment a site on their ordinary route.
terra: They also pass it by night and are asked whether they will reason; the ayah joins night travel to the failure to read what the eye sees.
luna: The section's source dictionary gives مَثَل the secondary sense of lesson; this ayah says the Qur'an sets out every kind of example for people so they may remember.

luna: The section's human calls abundance proof of honor; this ayah has a person say, after receiving favor, “I was given it because of knowledge,” then calls the favor a trial (فِتْنَة), exposing the same misreading. | terra: After harm, a human receives favor and says it came by his own knowledge; God calls it a test, exposing the inward gaze that misreads a changed condition.
luna: The section's present human repeats an old misreading of abundance; this continuation of 39:49 says earlier people made the same claim and were struck by the consequences of what they earned.
luna: The section's human calls a favor honor; following the claim in 39:49–50, this ayah says the evil they earned struck them, reversing their confidence in the favor.

luna: The section depicts a person judging honor by abundance; this ayah asks whether people know that God extends and measures provision for whom He wills, answering that judgment with divine choice. | terra: The question whether people know that God expands and restricts provision calls those changes signs, not independent proofs of honor or abasement.
terra: The disbelievers' movement through the lands must not deceive the addressee, repeating the warning that apparent freedom on the route is temporary.

luna: The section's watcher sees the passer before the passer sees him; this ayah says God knows the stealthy glance of the eyes and what breasts conceal, including what the observed person tries to hide. | terra: God knows the stealthy betrayal of eyes and what breasts conceal, uniting the outer eye, the inner condition, and the watcher neither can evade.

luna: The section links travel through countries to punishment of transgressors; this ayah asks people to travel and see that earlier, stronger peoples were seized for their sins. | terra: Travel through the earth would reveal how God seized peoples mightier and more marked in the land, closely echoing the observed ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh.

luna: The section makes ruined peoples evidence for the passing traveler; this ayah repeats the command to travel and see how earlier, stronger generations ended. | terra: Former peoples' greater numbers, force, and آثار did not avail them; their remains are meant to be seen by later travelers.
luna: After 41:12, this ayah warns that if people turn away they will face a thunderbolt like that of ʿĀd and Thamud, directly bringing the section's named peoples into a warning before judgment.

luna: The section's wording about guards before and behind the messenger (72:27) describes protective watch; here the phrase for messengers coming from before and behind describes repeated warnings across generations, not guards stationed around one messenger.

luna: The section names ʿĀd among those who transgressed in the lands; this ayah says they arrogantly claimed none was stronger than them, though their Creator was stronger. | terra: ʿĀd act arrogantly in the land and imagine no one stronger, a self-estimate that explains both their transgression and their failure to see the watcher.

luna: The section asks the reader to witness God's act against ʿĀd; this ayah says a furious wind brought them humiliating punishment in worldly life, while the Hereafter's punishment is more humiliating. | terra: A furious wind is sent against ʿĀd over ill-fated days so they taste disgrace, standing between their self-estimate in 41:15 and Thamūd's blinded choice in 41:17.

luna: The section's image turns on the difference between seeing and taking heed; this ayah says Thamud were shown guidance but chose blindness, then were seized by a humiliating blast. | terra: Thamūd prefer blindness over guidance, then the thunderbolt seizes them; failed inner sight and the observed blow form one causal scene.

luna: The section places the exposed wrongdoers beside the people who heed warning; this ayah says God saved those who believed and were mindful, marking the boundary between the punished and the protected.

luna: The section contrasts eyes that see with the hidden watcher's knowledge; this ayah says hearing, eyes, and skins testify when people reach the Fire, making their own faculties witnesses. | terra: At the Fire, hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners, so the person's own faculties become the watching evidence.

luna: The section says people fail to see the watcher before the strike; this ayah says they did not hide their hearing, eyes, and skins because they thought God did not know much of what they did. | terra: The sinners could not hide from their own hearing, eyes, and skins; 41:20 identifies these organs as the witnesses they failed to anticipate.

luna: After 41:22 exposes their assumption that God did not know, this ayah says that very thought ruined them, naming the cost of misreading the unseen watcher. | terra: Their false opinion about God's knowledge ruins them, showing inward judgment corrected by the watcher and bodily testimony in 41:20-22.
terra: After adversity, a person tastes mercy and says “this is mine” while dismissing the Hour, a direct instance of favor distorted by self-regard.
terra: Signs shown in the horizons and within people culminate in the Lord's witnessing of everything, moving from outer scene to inner recognition and then to divine watch.
terra: The keys of heaven and earth belong to God, who expands and restricts provision; the two conditions proceed from one sovereign measure.

luna: The section links excess provision with transgression in the lands; this ayah says that if God expanded provision to all servants they would البَغْيَ in the earth, while measured provision is sent as He wills, explaining the boundary behind the image. | terra: If provision were expanded without measure people would transgress, so God sends it in due measure and remains seeing of His servants; provision, limit-crossing, measure, and the watcher coincide.
terra: A human rejoices at mercy but becomes ungrateful when calamity follows his deeds, another exact contrast in inward responses to changing provision.

luna: The section's human takes provision as a personal verdict; this ayah says God apportions livelihood and raises some above others in degrees, so material differences are assigned provision, not proof of moral worth.

luna: The section describes the human who reads abundance as honor; Pharaoh points to Egypt's kingdom and rivers flowing beneath him as proof of his standing, joining wealth, land, and self-estimation.
luna: The section's human takes material ease as a verdict of honor; Pharaoh calls Moses contemptible and cites his lack of eloquence, exposing a ruler's false measure of worth.
terra: When Pharaoh's people provoke divine anger, God takes vengeance and drowns them all, the same observed divine action against a land-transgressor.

luna: The section's source dictionary gives مَثَل the sense of lesson; this ayah says the destroyed people were made a precedent and an example for those who came later, like the peoples shown in 89. | terra: Their destruction makes them a precedent and مَثَلًا for later people; the section's م ث ل branch as lesson is stated directly after the blow.

luna: The section extends the watch from the road to every spoken word; this ayah asks whether people think God does not hear their secrets and private conversations, then says messengers are present recording them. | terra: Secret and private speech is heard while messengers beside the speakers record it, closely paralleling the ready watcher over every utterance in 50:18.

luna: The section's source root س ر ي describes a group moving at night; Moses is again told to travel by night with God's servants, making the night route a repeated escape scene. | terra: The command to take God's servants by night because they will be followed repeats the section's س ر ي sense and leads the pursuers into the sea's blow.
luna: After Moses is told to leave at night in 44:23, this ayah tells him to leave the sea open because Pharaoh's host will drown in it, turning the route to safety into the pursuer's trap.
terra: The keepers are ordered to pour the punishment of boiling water over the sinner's head, another literal punitive ص ب ب from above.
terra: A person who takes desire as god has hearing and heart sealed and a covering placed over sight, depicting inward appetite disabling the eye's lesson.
terra: The book speaks truth against people because their actions were being transcribed, presenting the stored result of continuous observation.
terra: ʿĀd see the approaching cloud and read it as rain, although it is the punishment they hastened; their visual misreading concretely parallels the human's two false readings of one test.

terra: The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command until only dwellings can be seen, supplying the visible aftermath that the hearer of 89:6 is told to behold; 46:24 names the fatal misreading.

luna: The section's people are made to look at what happened to them; this ayah says hearing and eyes did not help the people of ʿĀd because they denied God's signs, showing that seeing alone is no protection. | terra: ʿĀd's hearing, eyes, and hearts avail them nothing despite their endowment, directly testing the section's distinction between possessing eyes and seeing with insight.
terra: God has destroyed towns around the audience and varied the signs so people might return, turning ʿĀd's sensory failure in 46:24-26 into a road-side warning for later observers.

luna: The section asks its listener to witness the outcome of earlier peoples; this ayah asks whether people traveled the land and saw how God destroyed those before them. | terra: The command to travel and see the old peoples' end says God destroyed them and promises the deniers comparable outcomes, making ruins an active warning.
terra: Two receivers sit on the right and left to take each deed, establishing the fixed observation-post specified as a ready watcher in 50:18.

luna: The section says the unseen watcher waits where everyone must pass; this verse places a ready observer beside every utterance, extending the image from a road to what a person says. | terra: Every utterance finds beside the speaker a ready watcher, رَقِيبٌ عَتِيدٌ, directly extending the section's watching eye to speech.

luna: The section's human may not notice the watcher until judgment; this ayah says every soul arrives with a driver and a witness, staging the final passage under observation. | terra: Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, moving the continually watched traveler into the judgment scene whose unveiled sight appears in 50:22.

luna: The section distinguishes looking with the eye from seeing with insight; this ayah says the veil is removed and sight is sharp on that day, reversing the earlier failure to recognize what was happening. | terra: At judgment the person's covering is removed and sight becomes sharp; this realizes the section's inward eye only when the concealed watch has reached its outcome.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss for ج و ب includes cutting across countries; this ayah says earlier, stronger peoples traversed the lands but found no place of escape, joining the route to the failure to outrun judgment. | terra: Destroyed generations stronger in force ranged through the lands but found no escape, an unusually close meeting of country-crossers, the waiting judgment, and the limit no traveler can pass.

luna: After 50:36 describes powerful generations searching the lands without escape, this ayah says the account is a reminder for a heart or an attentive listener, distinguishing travel from seeing with insight as in the section's source root رءي.
terra: Signs in the earth are offered to the certain before 51:21 turns the observing gaze into people's own selves.
terra: The signs are within people's own selves and the ayah asks أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ, an explicit inward turn of the seeing eye.
terra: The sending of the barren wind against ʿĀd gives another direct scene of the Lord's action that the observer of 89:6 is asked to see.
terra: The wind leaves everything it passes like ruins, supplying the visible aftermath of 51:41's divine act.
terra: Thamūd are granted enjoyment for a time before the thunderbolt of 51:44, making respite precede the blow in the same passage.
terra: Thamūd insolently cross their Lord's command and are seized by the thunderbolt while looking, bringing transgression, blow, and the victim's gaze together.
terra: Even if the deniers saw a piece of the sky falling, they would call it a piled cloud; their eye misreads an overhead blow as ordinary weather just as ʿĀd misread the approaching cloud.
terra: The messenger is told to wait patiently for the Lord's judgment because he is under God's eyes, making the watched position one of care while the decree ripens.

luna: The section links seeing (source root رءي) with transgression in the lands; here the Prophet's sight neither swerves nor exceeds its limit, a precise reversal of the transgressors' overstepping. | terra: مَا زَاغَ ٱلْبَصَرُ وَمَا طَغَىٰ describes sight that neither swerves nor crosses its bound, the direct opposite of both the source's double-seeing eye and rebellious limit-crossing.
terra: God destroys the former ʿĀd, directly naming the people whose fate the section tells the listener to see.
terra: God spares none of Thamūd, continuing the destruction of ʿĀd in 53:50 before 53:52 diagnoses Noah's people as still more transgressive.
terra: Noah's people are called more unjust and أَطْغَىٰ, repeating limit-crossing as the diagnosis of another destroyed people.
terra: The ark sails under God's eyes as recompense for Noah, showing the same divine watch as protective passage rather than capture.
luna: The section asks the listener to see what the Lord did to ʿĀd; this ayah repeats that ʿĀd denied and asks how severe the punishment and warning were.
luna: The section presents the blow falling on an overreaching people; this ayah describes the destructive wind sent against ʿĀd on an ill-fated day.
luna: The section's punished travelers are made to witness the force of the strike; this ayah says the wind tore people away as though they were uprooted palm trunks.
luna: The section presents the punishment as what an observer must recognize; this ayah again asks how severe the punishment and warning were for ʿĀd.
luna: The section names Thamud among the peoples made visible to the listener; this ayah says Thamud denied the warnings, setting up their own account of overstepping and punishment.
luna: The section links passage through the land to the fate of Thamud; this ayah says their she-camel is sent as a test for them, making their response to a divinely set limit the central scene.
luna: The section develops a watchpoint where every traveler must pass; this ayah assigns the camel and the people their separate turns at the water, a concrete boundary they must observe.
luna: The section describes a sudden blow following transgression; this ayah says the people called their companion, who seized the camel and hamstrung it, the act that brings the punishment.
luna: The section places the blow before the watchpoint is named; this ayah says a single cry was sent against Thamud and they became like dry stalks, completing the consequence of the broken limit.
terra: The command not to transgress in the balance gives ط غ ي a measured boundary rather than the old peoples' unchecked movement through the land.
luna: The section names those who exceeded limits in the lands; this ayah depicts a boundary between two seas that they do not cross, a specific reversal in which a limit is kept.
terra: Criminals are recognized by their marks and seized by forelocks and feet, so the watcher needs neither pursuit nor testimony to distinguish those arriving.
terra: At a person's death God is nearer than the gathered human observers, but they do not see; the unseen divine presence lies inside the visible watching scene.

luna: The section's human reads worldly abundance as honor; this ayah describes worldly life as adornment, boasting, and competition in wealth and children, then compares its growth to vegetation that withers.
terra: God has enumerated deeds that people forgot and is witness over everything, explaining how the patient watcher can disclose a complete record.
terra: The hearers are told to take lesson, O people of sight, after God reaches a fortified people from where they did not expect; hidden watching becomes visible outcome.
terra: Every soul is commanded to look at what it has sent forward for tomorrow while God remains aware of its deeds, joining self-inspection to the divine watcher.

luna: The section's source dictionary joins image (تمثال) and lesson (مثل); this ayah says that if the Qur'an were sent on a mountain, one would see it humbled and split from fear, then calls such comparisons a means to reflect.

luna: The section calls the test through provision ابتلاء; this ayah explicitly calls wealth and children a فِتْنَة and points to the greater reward with God, clarifying that possession is a trial. | terra: Possessions and children are again named as a test, while the great reward remains with God rather than in the visible abundance.
terra: The hearer is ordered to return the gaze over creation and ask whether any fissure can be seen, beginning the deliberate repeated looking opposed to a distorted self-view.
terra: The command to return sight كَرَّتَيْنِ gives the section's “eye looking two looks” a disciplined counterpart: repeated sight returns humbled and exhausted, not doubled into false judgments.
luna: The section's image of a flame watching the sky is stated here as lamps made missiles for devils, a second formulation of the same guarded heaven.
terra: People are told to walk through the earth's paths and eat God's provision, yet resurrection is to Him; route, measured livelihood, and unavoidable destination share one ayah.
terra: The addressees are asked whether they feel secure from the One above causing the earth to swallow them, one half of the above-and-below enclosure completed by 67:17.
terra: People are asked whether they feel secure from a storm of stones sent by the One above; its arrival would disclose the warning they ignored.
terra: The Creator produces people and grants hearing, eyes, and hearts, but little gratitude follows, echoing the unused capacities of ʿĀd.
terra: The garden owners are explicitly tested, linking an apparently secure abundance to the trial its possessors fail to recognize.
terra: They swear to harvest in the morning without making exception, displaying confidence in possession immediately before the unseen visitation.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while they sleep, a night-time watch and blow unknown to its owners.
terra: The garden becomes dark and stripped by morning, making the hidden visitation of 68:19 visible only in its result.
terra: God tells the messenger to leave the denier to Him, for He will lead such people gradually from where they do not know; the stationary watcher governs the approach.
terra: The respite granted after 68:44 rests on a firm plan, distinguishing delayed seizure from absence of observation.
luna: The section places ʿĀd and Thamud before the reader as witnessed peoples; this ayah names both as deniers of the striking calamity, directly recalling the same two communities.

luna: The section asks the reader to see what was done to ʿĀd and Thamud; this ayah says Thamud were destroyed by the overpowering blast, giving the event its force. | terra: Thamūd are destroyed by ٱلطَّاغِيَةِ, a calamity named with the ط غ ي root's overwhelming excess and placed beside ʿĀd's visible end.

luna: The section recalls the fate of ʿĀd; this ayah says ʿĀd were destroyed by a furious, violent wind, another account of what the observer is asked to see. | terra: ʿĀd are destroyed by a furious wind, placing the very people shown in 89:6 before the reader in another visible punishment scene.

luna: The section's punishment descends on a people who overstepped; this ayah describes the wind sent against ʿĀd for seven nights and eight days, exposing them as fallen trunks. | terra: The wind is imposed for seven nights and eight days so the people lie like hollow palm trunks, displaying the prolonged blow named in 69:6.

luna: The section makes the destroyed people an object of sight; this ayah asks whether any remnant of them can be seen after the wind, closing the visual account of ʿĀd. | terra: فَهَلْ تَرَىٰ لَهُم مِّنۢ بَاقِيَةٍ turns ʿĀd's disappearance into a direct question to the observer's eye.

luna: The section also names Pharaoh among the peoples exposed to judgment; this ayah groups Pharaoh and the overturned towns among those who committed error. | terra: Pharaoh and the overturned towns come with wrongdoing, continuing the observed catalogue from Thamūd and ʿĀd to the third ruler named by the section.

luna: The section names transgression in the lands before the punishment; this ayah says they disobeyed their Lord's messenger, so He seized them with an overwhelming seizure. | terra: They disobey their Lord's messenger, so He seizes them with an overwhelming seizure; this supplies the blow joining the peoples listed in 69:5-9.
terra: طَغَا ٱلْمَآءُ uses ط غ ي for water crossing its bound rather than rebellion, while the ark passes through the divinely controlled catastrophe.
terra: The rescue is made a reminder retained by a receptive ear; after 69:5-11 display the old peoples and the overflowing water, perception must turn the scene into a lesson.
terra: The human being is created anxiously grasping, introducing the unstable inward disposition behind the section's two judgments.
terra: When evil touches him he becomes impatient, specifying the deprivation-side response of the human described in 70:19.
terra: When good touches him he withholds it, completing the paired response and showing that abundance itself exposes rather than certifies him.

luna: Before 72:9's flame waiting for a listener, this ayah reports that the jinn found the sky filled with strong guards and flames, establishing the guarded passage that the section invokes. | terra: The jinn find heaven filled with strong guards and flames; this supplies the guarded terrain in which 72:9's waiting flame catches the seeker.

luna: The section names the root ر ص د and a serpent called رَصيد that waits for passers; the jinn find a شِهَابًا رَصَدًا waiting in the sky for anyone who tries to listen, a corresponding ambush from above. | terra: A jinn seeking a listening-place now finds a flame شِهَابًا رَصَدًا waiting for him, matching the traveler who discovers the watcher only when struck.

luna: After the jinn encounter the waiting flame in 72:9, this ayah records their uncertainty about whether harm or right guidance is intended for people, completing their response to the changed watch.

luna: The section's source root ر ص د names the watchers around a passage; here guards are placed before and behind God's messenger to protect what is revealed, making the watch protective rather than punitive. | terra: God places رَصَدًا before and behind an approved messenger; the same root depicts watchers stationed along a person's route rather than pursuing him.
terra: The guards of 72:27 serve a knowledge-and-accounting purpose: God encompasses what is with the messengers and counts everything, clarifying the watch rather than merely its position.
terra: On that day the human asks where escape lies, posing the road-traveler's question only after the hidden checkpoint has become visible.
terra: The answer says there is no refuge, closing every alternate route raised by 75:10.
terra: The final destination that day is to the Lord, completing the no-escape sequence with the place every traveler reaches.

luna: The section says the human looks at his own condition; this ayah calls the human a witness against himself, even if he offers excuses. | terra: ٱلْإِنسَانُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِۦ بَصِيرَةٌ makes the human being an inward witness against himself, the Quranic counterpart to the section's figure seen within the eye.
terra: God creates the human from a mixed drop to test him and makes him hearing and seeing, joining trial to the very faculties by which it should be read.

luna: The section's source dictionary form المِرْصاد (root ر ص د) names a watchpoint; this ayah calls Hell مرصادًا, turning the hidden waiting place into the destination that receives the travelers. | terra: Hell itself is called مِرْصَادًا, the same road-watchpoint named by the section; the next ayah identifies the transgressors for whom it waits.

luna: Following 78:21's Hell as a مِرْصاد (the section's source dictionary form under ر ص د), this ayah identifies the transgressors as those whose return is there; it names the people who meet the watchpoint. | terra: The next ayah identifies the transgressors as the destination for whom Hell waits; it completes 78:21's مِرْصَادًا without making the watchpoint morally indiscriminate.

luna: The section names Pharaoh among those who overstepped in the lands; Moses is told to go to him because he has transgressed, a second direct formulation of the same warning. | terra: Moses is sent to Pharaoh because إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ, the same limit-crossing in rebellion exemplified by the Pharaoh observed in the section.

luna: The section asks the listener to see what God did to earlier tyrants; this ayah says God seized Pharaoh with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first life, giving the ruler's end as an example. | terra: God seizes Pharaoh with an exemplary punishment for his latter and former claim, giving the delayed watcher’s decisive blow.

luna: The section makes a past ruler's fate a sight for the listener; this ayah calls Pharaoh's seizure a lesson for whoever fears, making the intended stance explicit. | terra: The seizure in 79:25 is explicitly an عِبْرَةً for one who fears, realizing the source dictionary's “parable as a lesson seen.”

luna: The section names those who crossed their limits in the lands; this ayah says the one who transgressed is among those whose end is being described. | terra: The one who طَغَىٰ is classified by the same act of exceeding the limit that characterizes the old peoples.

luna: After 79:37 identifies the transgressor, this ayah says he preferred worldly life, making that preference the particular inward choice behind the outcome. | terra: Preferring the nearer life supplies the inward valuation behind the transgression in 79:37.

luna: After the transgressor prefers worldly life in 79:38, this ayah names Hell as his refuge, reversing the security he thought his status gave him. | terra: Hell becomes that person's refuge, completing the transgressor-to-watchpoint sequence also stated in 78:21-22.
luna: The section's human makes a judgment from worldly conditions; this ayah contrasts him with the one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains his soul from desire.
luna: Following the restraint in 79:40, this ayah says the Garden is that person's refuge, giving the enduring outcome opposite the worldly preference.
terra: أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَآءَ صَبًّا uses the section's pouring root for life-giving rain, reversing the poured scourge while preserving the downward act.

luna: The section develops the watcher's presence at a passage; this verse says keepers are appointed over people, a direct parallel in the scene of unseen oversight. | terra: The statement that guardians stand over human beings makes the section's watcher a continuous presence over every traveler.

luna: The section's watcher observes those who pass; as a continuation of 82:10, this ayah identifies the keepers as noble recorders, specifying what their watch does. | terra: The guardians are noble recorders, specifying the kind of observer introduced in 82:10.

luna: The section's watcher is present before the traveler knows it; continuing 82:10–11, this ayah says the recorders know what people do, giving the watch its content. | terra: They know whatever people do, completing the stationary watch whose evidence appears when judgment arrives.
terra: The wicked are veiled from their Lord on that day, a boundary on human sight that does not limit the divine watcher who has seen them throughout.
terra: The person thought he would never return, yet his Lord was always seeing him; the ayah corrects 84:14's self-reading by disclosing the patient watcher.
terra: The One who owns heaven and earth is witness over everything, grounding the observing stance behind the severe seizure later named in 85:12.
terra: The Lord's grip is severe, giving the decisive blow that completes the universal witnessing of 85:9.

luna: The section's waiting watcher makes passage inescapable; this verse says every soul has a keeper over it, applying that oversight to each person. | terra: Every soul has a guardian over it, a concise universal form of the section's inescapable watching position.
terra: The opponents devise a plot, setting up the human attempt to control where and when another will be caught.
terra: God answers their plot with His own plan, disclosing the true watcher behind the apparent ambush of 86:15.
terra: The command to grant the disbelievers a little respite makes waiting part of the divine counter-plan rather than evidence that they escaped it.
luna: The section's human ranks himself by present ease; this ayah says people prefer the nearer life, naming the preference that turns temporary provision into their measure.
luna: After 87:16 names preference for the nearer life, this ayah says the Hereafter is better and more enduring, supplying the comparison that the section's human overlooks.
luna: The section's human makes a verdict from his worldly condition; this ayah asks whether he thinks no one can overpower him, beginning a portrait of false self-security.
luna: The section's human sees wealth as honor; this ayah has him boast that he spent abundant wealth, turning possession into self-display.
luna: The section's watcher is unseen until the traveler is struck; this ayah asks whether the boastful human thinks no one sees him, exposing the same false security.
terra: أَلَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُۥ عَيْنَيْنِ grounds the section's doubled-eye wordplay in the two eyes actually granted to the human being and for which he is accountable.

luna: The section names Thamud among those who transgressed; this ayah says Thamud denied in their rebellious excess (بِطَغْوَاهَا), making the same transgression the cause of their fate. | terra: Thamūd deny in their طَغْوَىٰ, attaching the section's limit-crossing word directly to one of its observed peoples.
luna: The section's watcher stands over travelers who cross a boundary; here the most wretched man rises to kill the she-camel after the warning, a boundary-breaking act before the punishment.
luna: The section develops an unseen watch and the blow that follows; Salih warns them not to harm God's she-camel or prevent her drink, a concrete limit they are about to cross.

luna: The section places a blow on transgressors before naming the watchpoint; this ayah says they hamstrung the camel and their Lord crushed them for their sin, connecting the broken limit to punishment. | terra: After hamstringing the camel, their Lord crushes and levels them for their sin, the decisive consequence of the transgression named in 91:11.

luna: The section's punishment leaves the powerful unable to escape the watcher; this ayah ends by saying God has no fear of the consequence, placing the human transgressors' exposure against divine power.

luna: The section says the human judges by how much provision he has; this ayah describes the one who withholds and sees himself as self-sufficient (اسْتَغْنَىٰ), a close parallel to 96:7 and the section's mistaken gaze. | terra: The person who is stingy and sees himself self-sufficient repeats the very inward estimate stated in 96:7.

luna: After describing the self-sufficient person in 92:8, this ayah says he denies the best outcome, connecting his self-estimation to his failure to heed the warning. | terra: He denies the finest truth, identifying the moral judgment joined to self-sufficiency in 92:8.

luna: After the person withholds and denies, this ayah says he will be eased toward hardship, reversing the assumption that present ease signals honor. | terra: He is eased toward hardship, a pointed reversal of the ease his wealth seemed to promise.

luna: This continuation says his wealth will not avail him when he falls, directly undoing the section's human claim that provision is his honor. | terra: His wealth will not avail him when he falls, making the final blow expose the false self-estimate of 92:8.

luna: The section connects people who crossed limits in the lands with a human judging himself by what he has; this ayah says the human transgresses (يَطْغَى), giving that overreach an inward cause. | terra: The declaration that the human being transgresses joins the section's ٱلْإِنسَانُ to its sense of طغيان as crossing the limit.

luna: The section says the human looks at his own condition and reads abundance as honor; this ayah locates the error in seeing oneself as self-sufficient (رَآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ). | terra: The human transgresses because he رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, sees himself self-sufficient; this is precisely the inward gaze that mistakes abundance for honor.
terra: أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ corrects the self-regarding person's view with the divine gaze that has watched throughout.

luna: The section's watcher records what passes before him; this ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making even the smallest deed visible. | terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, making deeds themselves the final object shown to the observed person.

luna: The section's unseen observer does not miss the passer; this ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, completing the reckoning of 99:7. | terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, completing the exact and morally differentiated disclosure at judgment.
terra: The human is himself a witness to his ingratitude, supporting the section's inward image of the person looking upon his own condition.
terra: His intense love of wealth names the attachment that distorts the self-witness in 100:7.
terra: Those distracted by competitive abundance will surely see Hell, shifting sight from the wealth they counted to the watchpoint they ignored.
terra: They will see it with the eye of certainty, the final sharpened gaze following 102:6's disclosure of Hell.
terra: The faulted person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, fixing his gaze on the very abundance by which he measures himself.
terra: He thinks his wealth makes him immortal, the most extreme form of reading provision as personal security.
terra: He will instead be hurled into the Crusher, the sudden destination that overturns the inward verdict in 104:3.

luna: The section's source root رءي frames 89:6 as making the listener witness what the Lord did; this repeats the same question and wording for the people of the Elephant, making an earlier event present to the reader. | terra: The exact summons أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ makes the hearer witness what the Lord did to the elephant army, just as 89:6 does with ʿĀd.
